title: David Bowie Wanted His Music to Sound Like This Painting Looks
standfirst: Frank Auerbach painted the same woman's head, weekly, for twenty-one years, scraping the paint off and starting again whenever a session went wrong. One of the results ended up in David Bowie's collection and sold for a record price. The sitter herself turns out to belong to a completely different, and far better documented, story of survival.

sections.heading: A Rock Star's Explanation for Owning a Head
sections.body: David Bowie bought this same title — Frank Auerbach made several works called *Head of Gerda Boehm*, and Bowie's was painted in 1965 — at Christie's in London on 26 May 1995. Three years later he tried to explain the attraction to *The New York Times*: looking at Auerbach's portraits, he said, could tip him toward depression or toward a kind of triumph, and what he wanted from his own records was simple — "[I want my music] to sound like that looks." He also said he could no longer tell, looking at the thick ridges of paint, whether he was looking at a painting or a piece of sculpture. When Bowie's estate consigned the picture to [Sotheby's in November 2016](https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2016/11/11/bidding-war-for-bowies-angst-ridden-auerbach-in-record-breaking-sale), against an estimate of £300,000–£500,000, six bidders pushed it to a hammer price of £3.25 million — £3.8 million with fees, a new auction record for Auerbach, set by a portrait of a woman almost nobody in the room had heard of.

sections.heading: The Only Relative He Had Left to Paint
sections.body: Frank Auerbach was born in Berlin in 1931 to Max Auerbach, a patent lawyer, and Charlotte Nora Borchardt, who had trained as an artist. He left Hamburg on a Kindertransport train on 4 April 1939 and reached Southampton three days later, [one of six children sponsored by the writer Iris Origo and her husband Antonio](https://www.thejc.com/news/obituaries/obituary-frank-auerbach-hspr3y54); his luggage, the same obituary notes, arrived neatly packed and labelled, a detail that says more about the parents left behind than any adjective could. Max and Charlotte were murdered in a Nazi camp in 1942 — [the Sainsbury Centre's own catalogue entry names it as Auschwitz](https://sainsburycentre.ac.uk/art-and-objects/50635-head-of-gerda-boehm/), though the Jewish Chronicle's obituary states plainly that Auerbach himself never discovered which camp it was. His cousin Gerda Boehm, who had already got out to England with her husband, became the one relative he had left. She first sat for him in 1961 and kept sitting, in weekly sessions, until 1982.

sections.heading: Two Boys on the Same Berlin Street
sections.body: Gerda and Frank had been neighbours before any of this: the Reich family lived at Güntzelstrasse 53 in Berlin's Bayerisches Viertel, the Auerbachs at number 49. [As a sixteen-year-old schoolboy, Gerda's younger brother sometimes babysat the young Frank](https://www.tagesspiegel.de/berlin/bezirke/nachbarn-im-berliner-kiez-als-marcel-reich-ranicki-der-babysitter-von-frank-auerbach-war-11091952.html) for one or two marks an evening, reading through the hours while the child, he later recalled, never once woke up. That brother was Marcel Reich-Ranicki, who would become West Germany's most powerful literary critic — and Gerda Reich, [born in Włocławek in 1907](https://www.stolpersteine-berlin.de/de/guntzelstr/53/helene-reich), was his sister, married by the time of the paintings to a Gerhard Böhm. Sources disagree on when she and her husband got out — 1938 by one account, 1939 by another — but agree on what happened to the rest of that family: their parents were deported to Treblinka in September 1942, their brother Alexander, a dentist, was shot at the Poniatowa labour camp in 1943, and Marcel himself survived by escaping the Warsaw Ghetto and hiding until liberation. A letter [from Marcel to "his sister Gerda Boehm", dated 29 June 1945](https://www.dnb.de/DE/Ueber-uns/Presse/ArchivPM2022/_content/2022Download02BilderMRR_textbaustein.html), survives in a private collection — written weeks after the war in Europe ended, to the one sibling who had made it out. As adults, the cousins reportedly found conversation hard going: one fluent in literature and music, the other in paint, with little common ground between them despite the shared street and the shared losses.

sections.heading: Bury the Irrelevant
sections.body: Auerbach trained at St Martin's and the Royal College of Art, but the influence he named as decisive was David Bomberg, whose evening classes at Borough Polytechnic he attended from 1947 to 1953 alongside Leon Kossoff. [Wikipedia's account of his method](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Auerbach) describes a painter who would build up a picture in a single sitting, then, dissatisfied, scrape the paint off the board entirely and begin again the next week — a cycle repeated for months before he judged a canvas finished. "I never visualise a picture before I start," [he told the Sainsbury Centre](https://sainsburycentre.ac.uk/art-and-objects/50635-head-of-gerda-boehm/); "I have an impulse and I try to find a form for that impulse." His earliest attempts at Gerda's head, in charcoal, were reworked so hard that the paper itself tore and had to be collaged back together — [images "scarred and distressed by the fury of their working"](https://www.sothebys.com/en/digital-catalogues/london-an-artistic-crossroads/head-of-gerda-boehm-frank-auerbach-sainsbury-centre), as the same catalogue puts it, evoking the real distress behind them. By the oils, the paint itself had become the argument: applied in thick coils that dried like meringue, defended by Auerbach on another occasion with a line that could stand for the whole practice — ["Nothing can be left out… you have to bury the irrelevant in the painting somehow."](https://www.clevelandart.org/art/1982.38) None of this makes him an Expressionist in any working sense; historians group him with the School of London, alongside early supporters Francis Bacon and Lucian Freud, not with any European Expressionist lineage. The label on a database is a filing convenience, not a critical judgment.

sections.heading: One Title, Repeated Until It Stopped Meaning One Painting
sections.body: Because the sittings ran for two decades, "Head of Gerda Boehm" is not the name of a single object. A 1964 version hangs at the Sainsbury Centre in Norwich, [accepted by the UK government in lieu of inheritance tax and allocated there only in 2015](https://sainsburycentre.ac.uk/art-and-objects/50635-head-of-gerda-boehm/) — a family, at some point, settling a tax bill with a painting rather than cash. A 1981 version belongs to the Cleveland Museum of Art, [bought in 1982 through the Mr. and Mrs. William H. Marlatt Fund](https://www.clevelandart.org/art/1982.38). Bowie's 1965 version is now somewhere in a private collection again, sold on for a sum that would have meant nothing to the woman who sat for it every week for the ordinary reason that her cousin had almost no one else left to paint. This particular reproduction carries no date in the record it comes from — one more head, among several, of a woman whose name most people who now own a piece of her would need to look up.
